title: Five friends, truth-tellers and liars
intro: Five friends, A, B, C, D and E, are each either a truth-teller, who always tells the truth, or a liar, who always lies. Each of them makes one statement.
clues: A: "D and E are both truth-tellers."
B: "A is a liar."
C: "A and E are of different types."
D: "Exactly one of A and C is a truth-teller."
E: "At least one of B and D is a truth-teller."

questions.stem: How many of the five friends are truth-tellers?
why: A tells the truth (see the walkthrough), so D and E do too; B's and C's statements are false.
A, D and E are truth-tellers: 3.

questions.stem: Who are the liars?
why: A is a truth-teller, so D and E are truth-tellers too.
B's claim that A is a liar is false, and C's claim that A and E differ is false. The liars are B and C.

questions.stem: Suppose A's statement is ignored (A says nothing), while the other four statements stay as they are. How many different assignments of truth-teller and liar to the five friends are then consistent with the four statements?
why: Split on A. If A is a truth-teller, B is a liar; C tells the truth exactly when E lies; D tells the truth exactly when C lies; and E tells the truth exactly when D does. So D and E are of one kind and C the other: the truth-tellers are A, D, E or A, C.
If A is a liar, B tells the truth, so E does (B is one), C does (A and E differ) and D does (exactly one of A and C): B, C, D, E.
That is 3 assignments.

questions.stem: Suppose E's statement is changed to "C is a truth-teller" and the other four statements stay as they are. Who is then the only truth-teller?
why: If E told the truth, C would too, so A and E differ and A lies; D's statement would then be true, and A's ("D and E are both truth-tellers") true as well, against A lying. So E lies.
Then C lies, so A and E are of the same type: A lies. B says A is a liar: true, so B tells the truth. D says exactly one of A and C tells the truth: false. B is the only truth-teller.

questions.stem: Suppose B's statement is changed to "Exactly 2 of the 5 of us are liars" and the other four statements stay as they are. How many of the five are then truth-tellers?
why: If A told the truth, D and E would too and C would lie; then B's "exactly 2 liars" is false if B tells the truth, and true if B lies. Either way it fails, so A lies.

If E told the truth, A's false statement makes D a liar, D's false statement makes C the same type as A (a liar), and C's false statement makes A and E the same type: but A lies and E does not. So E lies.
E's false statement makes B and D liars, D's makes C a liar, and C's false statement fits A and E both lying. All five lie, and B's "exactly 2" is false, as it should be: 0 truth-tellers.

steps: Take A's statement and try both cases: A a truth-teller (the statement is true) or a liar (it is false). Follow each case until it breaks.

If A tells the truth, D and E do too. B's "A is a liar" is false, so B lies; C's "A and E differ" is false, so C lies. D's statement (exactly one of A and C) is true and E's (B or D) is true. Everything fits.

If A lies, B tells the truth, so E (at least one of B and D) tells the truth; A's false statement then makes D a liar, D's false statement makes C a liar, and C's "A and E differ" becomes true: a contradiction. So A tells the truth, and the answer is unique.

diagram.note: Try one person's statement both ways and follow it until it breaks.

title: Truth-tellers, liars and alternators
intro: Four people, A, B, C and D, each make two statements, one after the other. There are three kinds of person. A truth-teller makes two true statements. A liar makes two false statements. An alternator makes one true and one false statement, in either order (the order is not known in advance).
clues: A, first: "B and D are of different kinds."
A, second: "C is not a truth-teller."
B, first: "C is not an alternator."
B, second: "D is a truth-teller."
C, first: "A and D are of different kinds."
C, second: "Exactly 3 of the 4 of us are liars."
D, first: "Exactly 2 of the 4 of us are liars."
D, second: "B is a liar."

questions.stem: Who is the liar?
why: B cannot tell the truth: D would be a truth-teller, and D's "B is a liar" would be true.
B as an alternator fails too (see the walkthrough), so B is the liar: A tells the truth, and C and D are alternators.

questions.stem: How many of the eight statements are true?
why: A's two are true (2), B's two false (0), C's first true and second false (1), D's first false and second true (1).

questions.stem: Which person is an alternator who made a false statement first and a true statement second?
why: D's first statement (exactly 2 liars) is false, since only B lies; D's second (B is a liar) is true. So D lied first.
C is the alternator who told the truth first; A is a truth-teller and B a liar.

questions.stem: Suppose B's first statement had been "C is an alternator" instead (everything else unchanged). Then who is the liar?
why: B is still not a truth-teller. If B lied, C would not be an alternator, D would be an alternator who lied first, C would have to be a liar and A an alternator; but A's two statements both come out true, so A would be a truth-teller: a contradiction.

So B is an alternator: D is not a truth-teller, and B's first statement is the true one, so C is an alternator. D cannot be an alternator (D's second statement is false, and "exactly 2 liars" cannot then be true), so D is the liar, and A, with two true statements, is a truth-teller.

questions.stem: Suppose D's first statement had been "Exactly 1 of the 4 of us is a liar" instead (everything else unchanged). How many of the four are alternators?
why: If B lied, the reasoning of the walkthrough makes B the only liar, and then D's new first statement (exactly 1 liar) would be true, though D lied first: a contradiction. So B is an alternator.

A liar D forces three liars (A, C, D), which makes C's second statement true: impossible. So D is an alternator who told the truth first, with exactly one liar, C; C's false first statement makes A and D the same kind.
A, B and D are alternators: 3.

steps: Two statements with the same truth value belong to a truth-teller or a liar; two with different values belong to an alternator. Every pair of statements has to match its speaker's kind.
B cannot be a truth-teller: B's second statement would make D one, and D's "B is a liar" would then be true.

If B lies: C is an alternator and D is not a truth-teller. D's "B is a liar" is true, so D is an alternator who lied first. With two alternators there cannot be 3 liars, so C's second statement is false and C's first is true: A and D differ. A's two statements come out true, so A is a truth-teller. This fits.

If B is an alternator: B's second statement is false, so the first is true and C is a truth-teller or a liar. A truth-teller C would need 3 liars, which there cannot be, so C lies and A and D are the same kind. A liar D gives three liars and makes C's second statement true; an alternator D needs exactly two liars with only C lying. Both fail, so B is the liar.

diagram.note: Each person's two statements must match their kind: both true, both false, or one of each.

title: Five friends and their birth months
intro: Five friends, P, Q, R, S and T, were born in five different months of the same year: January, March, April, June and September, not necessarily in that order. Each friend made one statement about the birth months. A friend whose statement is true is a truth-teller; a friend whose statement is false is a liar. Exactly three of the five friends are truth-tellers.
"Exactly k months apart" means the month numbers differ by k: March and June are 3 months apart. "Earlier" and "later" refer to the order within the year.
clues: P: "Q and S were born exactly 2 months apart."
Q: "S is the latest-born of the five."
R: "Q and T were born exactly 5 months apart."
S: "S and T were born exactly 2 months apart."
T: "Q and P were born exactly one month apart."

questions.stem: In which month was R born?
why: Q's statement is false and S is the second liar (see the walkthrough). R's and T's true statements give Q April, P March and T September; P's gives S June.
January is left, so R was born in January.

questions.stem: By how many months does the birth of P differ from the birth of T?
why: P was born in March (3) and T in September (9).

questions.stem: Who are the liars?
why: With P March, Q April, R January, S June and T September: P's statement (April and June, 2 apart) is true; Q's (S latest) is false, as T is later; R's (April and September, 5 apart) is true; S's (June and September, 3 apart) is false; T's (April and March, 1 apart) is true.
The liars are Q and S.

questions.stem: If the five friends are lined up in the order of their birth, earliest first, in which position does Q stand?
why: The order is R (January), P (March), Q (April), S (June), T (September).
Q is third.

questions.stem: Suppose instead that exactly two of the five statements are true, and Q's statement ("S is the latest-born") is one of them. In how many different ways can the five months be assigned to the five friends?
why: Q's statement true puts S in September. Then P's and S's statements are false (no month is 2 from September), so exactly one of R's and T's is true.
R's true: Q and T are January and June (2 orders), P and R fill March and April (2 ways): 4, and T's statement is then false.
T's true: Q and P are March and April (2 orders), R and T fill January and June (2 ways): 4, and R's is then false. 4 + 4 = 8.

steps: Turn each statement into month numbers: January 1, March 3, April 4, June 6, September 9. Exactly 2 apart allows only January-March and April-June; exactly 5 apart only January-June and April-September; one apart only March-April.

If Q's statement were true, S would be September, and P's and S's statements would be false, leaving R's and T's both true: Q and T would be January and June, and Q and P March and April. Q cannot be in both pairs, so Q lies, and exactly one other friend lies.

Try each of P, R, S and T as the second liar. With R lying, S and T cannot be 2 apart; with P lying, S and T cannot be 2 apart either; with T lying, S and T always come out 3 apart. Only S lying works.
So R's and T's statements are true: Q April, P March, T September. P's makes S June, and R takes January.

diagram.note: Months as numbers: January 1, March 3, April 4, June 6, September 9.

title: Six friends at a round table, two of them liars
intro: Six friends, P, Q, R, S, T and U, sit at a round table with six equally spaced seats, all facing the centre. Each friend makes one statement about the seating. Exactly two of the six are liars; the other four tell the truth.
"Immediately to X's left" is the seat next to X on X's left-hand side as X faces the centre; "second to X's left" is the seat beyond that. The right-hand versions are defined the same way.
clues: P: "U sits immediately to P's left."
Q: "T sits immediately to Q's left."
R: "U sits second to T's right."
S: "R sits immediately to S's left."
T: "R sits immediately to T's right."
U: "Q sits second to U's left."

questions.stem: Who sits opposite P?
why: The only seating, clockwise from P, is P, U, Q, T, S, R (see the walkthrough).
The seat opposite P is the fourth from P: T.

questions.stem: How many of the six statements are true?
why: Exactly two friends lie, T and U: the seat to T's right holds Q, not R, and the seat second to U's left holds T, not Q.
P's, Q's, R's and S's statements are true: 4.

questions.stem: Who sits immediately to R's right?
why: Facing the centre, a person's right is the next seat anticlockwise (seen from above). Clockwise from P the seats are P, U, Q, T, S, R, so the seat anticlockwise of R is S.
This also agrees with S's true statement: R sits immediately to S's left.

questions.stem: Number the seats 1 to 6 clockwise as seen from above, starting with P in seat 1. In which seat does S sit?
why: S sits in seat 5.

questions.stem: Suppose it is also known that P is one of the two liars. How many seating arrangements are possible?
why: Exactly one seating fits "exactly two liars", and in it P tells the truth.
So if P must lie, no seating works: 0.

steps: Number the seats clockwise as seen from above. Facing the centre, a person's left-hand neighbour is the next seat clockwise and the right-hand neighbour the next anticlockwise. Only relative places matter, so put P in seat 1.
R's and U's statements cannot both be true: R's puts U two seats to T's right, so T is two seats clockwise of U; U's puts Q two seats clockwise of U too. So at least one of R and U lies.
If both R and U lie, the other four tell the truth, and Q's and T's statements put R in Q's seat: impossible. So exactly one of R and U lies, and one more friend lies.
If U lies and R tells the truth, the second liar has to be T (any other choice puts two friends in one seat): P 1, U 2 (P's statement), T 4 (R's), Q 3 (Q's), and R 6, S 5 (S's).
If R lies and U tells the truth, every choice of the second liar puts two friends in one seat or leaves no room. So the seating is unique: clockwise P, U, Q, T, S, R, with T and U lying.

diagram.note: Seat numbers run clockwise from P, the way a person facing the centre turns to the left.
